Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-10-13](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-10-13).

AmphibiaWeb lists 8,018 frog and toad species, and for most of them it lists one country.
That is true of 5,985 species, or 75%.
So the interesting question is where.

Islands far from any mainland keep almost all of their frogs.
Madagascar has 443 species and 440 of them live nowhere else, and 296 of those belong to one family, the Mantellidae.
Six of the nine remote islands keep more than 80% of their species.
Papua New Guinea and Indonesia sit lower, at 78% and 59%, and they share the island of New Guinea with each other.
Islands close to a mainland look like the mainland instead: Singapore keeps one species out of 28.

Large mainland countries mostly share.
Bolivia has 262 species and keeps 76.
The rest are shared with other countries, and the five it shares the most with are Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Ecuador and Argentina.
Of the 76 mainland countries on the plot, 56 keep under a quarter of their species, and none keeps 75% or more.
Brazil is the largest case, with 1,173 species, and it keeps 837 of them, which is 71%.

Whole families can be local too.
Eight families live in one country only, among them Brachycephalidae with 84 species in Brazil, Micrixalidae with 24 in India, and Ranixalidae with 19 in India.
Mantellidae is almost in that group, with 296 of its 300 species in Madagascar.

Some cautions.
AmphibiaWeb's country lists can be incomplete, and a species that is missing from a list looks more local than it is.
"Found in no other country" means one ISO code in the data, not an expert assessment of endemism.
The island groups were set by hand.
